entries.meaning: The delighted residents of Prayāga—forest hermits, religious students, householders, and renunciants—gathered in small groups and spoke of Bharata’s true, pure love and character. Hearing Rāma’s lovely virtues, Bharata came before the eminent Bharadvāja and prostrated. The sage regarded him as fortune embodied, ran to raise and embrace him, blessed him, and made him fulfilled. Bharata accepted a seat with bowed head, so hesitant that he seemed to have fled into a house. Before he could ask, the sage perceived his reserve and said: ‘Bharata, we know the whole matter; no one has power over destiny’s acts. Do not blame yourself after considering your mother’s deed. Dear child, Kaikeyī too is not at fault: a divine utterance bewildered her understanding.’

Bharadvāja continued: ‘Though saying even this may seem improper, both worldly judgment and the Vedas agree. By singing your spotless fame, both the world and sacred tradition will themselves gain honor. All acknowledge that the son to whom his father gives a kingdom should receive it. The truth-vowed king summoned you and would have bestowed kingship, happiness, duty, and renown. Rāma’s forest journey, which pierced the whole world with pain, occurred because the unwise queen was mastered by destiny; after plotting badly, she repented in the end. Whoever assigns even a little fault to you is base, ignorant, and unholy. Even had you accepted the throne, you would have been blameless and Rāma would have rejoiced to hear it. What you have now done is especially good; love for Raghubara’s feet is the root of every blessing.’

The sage told Bharata: ‘That love is your wealth, life, and very breath; who can equal your immense good fortune? This is no wonder in Daśaratha’s son, Rāma’s beloved brother. Hear me: in Raghubara’s heart no vessel of love equals you. Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa spent the whole night praising you. I learned the secret while they bathed at Prayāga: they become immersed whenever your affection is recalled. Raghubara’s love for you is what happiness, life, fame, and consciousness are to ordinary people. This does not chiefly magnify Rāma, protector of every family that seeks refuge; rather, Bharata, in my judgment you are Rāma’s love embodied. What seems a stain upon you instructs us all and has become an auspicious opportunity for attaining the nectar and perfection of devotion to Rāma.’

‘Dear Bharata, your spotless fame is a new moon for the water-lilies and cakora birds who serve Raghubara. It will remain forever risen, never set or wane, but grow twofold day by day in the world’s sky. Though the cakravākas of all three worlds will love it greatly, the sunlike splendor of the Lord’s majesty will not steal its beauty; it will give joy to everyone day and night, and the Rāhu of Kaikeyī’s deed will never swallow it. Full of the nectar of Rāma’s pure love and unstained by the fault of dishonoring the guru, you have made immortality readily available upon earth so Rāma’s devotees may drink their fill. King Bhagīratha brought the Gaṅgā, a mine of blessings when remembered; Daśaratha’s host of virtues cannot be described, for none in the world equals the one whose constrained love brought Rāma visibly before eyes that behold him without satiety.’

Bharadvāja said: ‘You have made an incomparable moon of fame in which Rāma’s love dwells like a deer-mark. Let shame leave your heart; fearing after receiving such love would be like a pauper fearing the philosopher’s stone. We do not speak falsely—we are detached ascetics of the forest. The lovely fruit of all our disciplines was the sight of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, and Sītā, and the fruit of that fruit is seeing you; Prayāga and I are fortunate. Blessed Bharata, your fame has conquered the world.’ Overcome by love, the sage fell silent. The assembly rejoiced; holy people praised Bharata and gods rained flowers. Cries of ‘Blessed!’ filled Prayāga’s sky, and Bharata sank deeper into love. His body thrilled, Rāma and Sītā filled his heart, and his lotus eyes grew wet; bowing to the circle of sages, he spoke in a choked voice.

Bharata replied: ‘Before this assembly of sages and the king of holy places, I swear truly that embellishing anything would be a dreadful and base sin. You are omniscient, and I speak sincerely: Raghurāya knows the heart within. I do not grieve over my mother’s deed, nor because the world may think me vile. I do not fear damage to the next world, and I do not mourn my father’s death: he filled the worlds with merit and fair fame and gained sons like Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. He cast off his perishable body in separation from Rāma—what occasion is there to grieve for such a king? My pain is that Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā wander forest after forest in ascetic dress, barefoot, wearing deerskin, eating fruit, sleeping upon earth on spread leaves and kuśa, living beneath trees, and daily enduring cold, heat, rain, and wind.’

‘The burning of this sorrow scorches my chest day and night; I have neither hunger by day nor sleep by night. I searched the whole world within my mind and found no medicine for this grievous disease. My mother’s evil intention is the carpenter and sin its root; pretending to serve me, she fashioned the adze. From the bad timber of the Kali age she made an evil mechanism, planted the fixed term as a post, and recited the hard, wicked counsel. For my sake she contrived this ruin and scattered the whole world to the twelve roads. The evil conjunction can end only when Rāma returns and dwells in Ayodhyā; there is no other remedy.’ Bharadvāja delighted in Bharata’s words and praised him in many ways: ‘Dear child, do not grieve excessively; every sorrow will vanish when you see Rāma’s feet.’ Consoling him, the sage lovingly asked him to accept tubers, roots, fruit, and flowers as a guest.

Hearing the sage, Bharata inwardly worried that the moment was ill-suited for hospitality and felt severe embarrassment. But recognizing the guru’s weighty command, he bowed at his feet and said with joined hands: ‘I shall place your order upon my head; this is our highest duty, Lord.’ His words pleased Bharadvāja, who called pure attendants and disciples and ordered them to welcome Bharata by fetching tubers, roots, and fruit. Saying, ‘Very well, Lord,’ they bowed and gladly went about their tasks. The sage reflected that the guest and invitation were great, so the worship should match the deity. At this, Prosperity, Perfection, and the supernatural powers such as aṇimā appeared and asked what they should do. The delighted sage-king ordered them to honor Bharata, his younger brothers, and the company—distraught in separation from Rāma—and remove their fatigue.

Prosperity and the supernatural powers received the eminent sage’s command upon their heads and counted themselves greatly fortunate. Their whole company said among themselves: ‘Our incomparable guest is Rāma’s younger brother. Bowing to the sage’s feet, today let us make the entire royal company happy.’ They created many beautiful residences whose sight would put celestial vehicles to shame and filled them with abundant pleasures and splendor that even immortals desired upon seeing. Maidservants, servants, and every appointment stood attentive, inwardly giving their whole minds to their guests. In a moment the powers adorned the entire camp with joys unavailable even in heaven or dreams. First they gave everyone a lovely, comfortable lodging suited to individual taste. Then the sage invited Bharata and his family to enter the astonishing wealth produced by his ascetic power.

When Bharata saw the sage’s power, the realms of all the guardians of the worlds seemed small. The company’s pleasures cannot be described; even wise renunciants would forget detachment at the sight. There were seats, beds, fine garments, canopies, gardens and groves, many birds and deer, fragrant flowers, nectar-like fruits, and varied pure pools. Food and drink were clean and nectar-sweet, and people hesitated before them as though embarrassed by the earth. Divine cows and wish-fulfilling trees served everyone; even Indra and Śacī’s wishes could be read there. Spring prevailed, a threefold breeze blew, and all four human aims were readily available. Garlands, sandalwood, women, and other pleasures filled people with joy and wonder. Prosperity was a female cakravāka, Bharata its mate, and the sage’s command the player directing them; that night the hermitage held them within a cage, until dawn arrived.
